title: When Pool Equipment and Plumbing Leaks Reach the House | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: A homeowner guide to pool pump, filter and underground plumbing leaks that migrate into a Phoenix home, and how to trace the water back to its source.
h1: When Pool Equipment and Plumbing Leaks Find Their Way Into the House
breadcrumbLabel: Pool Equipment Leaks Into the Home
intro: You have probably walked past that damp spot more than once. The baseboard in the back bedroom that feels cool to the touch. The tile grout along the patio door that never quite dries. The section of carpet near the wall that darkens a little, then lightens, then darkens again with no rain in sight. You mopped it. You ran a fan on it. You told yourself it was the mop water, or the dog, or the kids coming in from the pool. And then it came back, and it kept coming back, and somewhere in there the question stopped being what is this and started being why does this keep happening to my house. That is a heavy thing to carry quietly. It is also, very often, a sign that water is arriving from somewhere you have not thought to look yet.

sections.heading: Why a pool problem can show up inside the house
sections.body:
A swimming pool is a plumbing system that happens to be outdoors. Water leaves the pool through the skimmer and main drain, travels through buried suction lines to the pump, gets pushed through the filter and heater, and returns through buried pressure lines back to the pool wall. Most of that piping runs underground, and a lot of it runs alongside or under a patio slab that shares a footing with your house.

When a pressure line develops a crack, the pump is actively forcing water into the soil every hour the system runs. That is not a slow drip. In Phoenix soils, saturated ground does not just sit there. Water follows the path of least resistance, which is usually the trench the pipe was laid in, then the gravel bed under the patio, then the gap where the slab meets the foundation. From there it wicks up through the slab edge into the bottom of the drywall and the underside of the flooring. The pool level drops a little, you top it off with the autofill without thinking about it, and the only evidence you ever see is a damp baseboard on the inside of the house.

Equipment pad leaks work the same way, just closer to the surface. A weeping pump seal, a cracked filter housing, a failed backwash valve or a heater that drips when it cycles can put water into the ground within a few feet of the house day after day.

sections.heading: Signs the water is coming from outside, not from a fixture inside
sections.body:
Before you open a wall, it is worth spending an afternoon narrowing down where the water is entering. A few things separate an exterior source from an interior supply or drain leak:

The damage is low and at an exterior wall. Water from pool plumbing and equipment usually enters at the slab edge, so the wet drywall starts at the floor and moves up. A supply line leak inside a wall generally starts higher and runs down.

It tracks with the pump schedule. If the damp area is worse in the afternoon after the pump has run all day and drier in the morning, that points at a pressure-side line.

The pool loses more water than evaporation explains. Do a bucket test: fill a bucket with pool water, set it on a step so it is partly submerged, mark the water level inside and outside the bucket, turn off the autofill, and compare after 24 hours. Evaporation affects both equally. If the pool drops more than the bucket, the pool is losing water somewhere.

The equipment pad is never dry. Look for a rust ring under the pump motor, mineral crust on threaded fittings, a wet patch of decomposed granite that stays dark, or efflorescence (white powder) on nearby block wall.

There is a musty smell with no visible source. Water inside a wall cavity or under a floating floor will smell before it shows. In closed-up Arizona houses running the AC, that smell tends to concentrate in one room.

Flooring is telling on itself. Tile that sounds hollow when tapped, wood that cups or crowns at the plank edges, vinyl plank that lifts at a seam, or carpet tack strip that has rusted through are all slab moisture symptoms.

sections.heading: Steps that help before anyone opens a wall
sections.body: Turn the pump off. Not on a timer, off at the breaker. If the leak is on the pressure side, the pump is the thing driving water into the ground, and stopping it stops the volume immediately. Shut the autofill valve too so the pool level can tell you the truth. Watch the level. Mark the tile line with a piece of tape. If the pool keeps dropping with the pump off, the leak is likely on the suction side or in the shell. If it stops dropping, you are looking at the pressure side or the equipment. Get air moving inside. Pull baseboard away if it is already loose, lift the edge of an area rug, open interior doors and run the AC. Do not put plastic sheeting over a damp area, because that traps moisture against the material. Take pictures with dates. Photograph the wet area, the equipment pad, the pool level marks and anything you moved. If this becomes an insurance conversation later, a record of how the damage progressed is worth more than a description from memory. Do not paint or seal over it. Sealing a damp slab edge or repainting stained drywall hides the signal without removing the moisture, and the material behind it keeps deteriorating. Understand the two halves of the repair. Fixing the leak is plumbing and pool work. Drying the structure and rebuilding what the water ruined is a different scope, covering moisture readings inside wall cavities and under flooring, controlled removal of unsalvageable material, and then putting drywall, trim, paint and flooring back. Both halves have to happen, and doing only the first leaves wet material in the wall.

sections.heading: Why slow water does more damage than a burst pipe
sections.body: A pipe that bursts is loud, obvious and gets attention within hours. A pool line seeping under a patio can run for months or years, and that is the version that quietly costs more. Slow, repeated wetting gives mold time to establish in the paper facing of drywall, in the back of baseboard, and in the pad under carpet. It gives wood framing and door jambs time to swell and soften. In hard-water areas, it can leave mineral deposits inside the slab that keep drawing moisture even after the leak is fixed. Concrete itself does not rot, but everything attached to it does. There is also the part that is harder to talk about: living with a problem you cannot name is exhausting. Repainting the same corner, moving furniture off the same three feet of floor, wondering whether you are imagining the smell. If you have been doing that for a while, you are not being dramatic and you did not miss something obvious. Underground leaks are genuinely hard to see, which is exactly why they get to run so long. When you are ready to have someone look at the inside damage, water damage restoration starts with mapping how far the moisture actually traveled, which is usually further than the visible stain. faqs.q: Can a pool leak really damage the inside of my house?
faqs.a: Yes. Pool return and suction lines are usually buried, and many of them run within a few feet of the house along a patio slab. Water forced into the soil by the pump follows the pipe trench and the gravel under the slab, then wicks up at the slab edge into baseboard, drywall and flooring. The pool level barely moves because the autofill keeps topping it off, so the first thing many homeowners notice is a damp wall inside.

faqs.q: How do I tell a pool plumbing leak from a slab leak in my house plumbing?
faqs.a: A useful first test is to turn the pool pump off at the breaker and close the autofill for a day or two. If the damp area inside dries out and the pool level holds, the pool system is the likely source. If the pool keeps dropping with the pump off, the leak is on the suction side or in the shell. If the interior damp spot stays wet regardless of the pump, look at household supply lines, and check your water meter with every fixture off to see whether it is still turning.

faqs.q: The wall is only a little damp. Do I need to open it up?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but you do need to know what is behind it. Surface dampness at a baseboard often means the bottom plate and the back of the drywall are wetter than the face you can see, and insulation in that cavity can hold water for a long time. Moisture meters and cavity probes answer that without demolition. If readings come back dry behind the surface, you dry what is there. If they come back wet, removing a strip of drywall is far less work than replacing a whole wall later.

faqs.q: Will my homeowners insurance cover pool equipment leak damage?
faqs.a: That depends on your policy and on how the damage happened, and only your carrier can answer it. In general terms, policies tend to treat a sudden failure differently from long-term seepage that went unaddressed, and the pool equipment itself is often handled separately from damage to the house. Document the damage with dated photos, keep any repair invoices, and report it to your carrier before work starts rather than after.
